response.query: What Monte Carlo parameters (effect sizes, ICCs, cluster sizes) yield adequate power for small/medium/large effects in team-level designs, and what minimal team counts do they imply?
response.answer: For small effects, large sample sizes and high ICCs are needed; medium effects require moderate sample sizes; large effects need smaller sample sizes. Minimum team counts vary based on desired power and ICC.

results.title: Effect sizes and intra-cluster correlation coefficients measured from the Green Dot High School study for guiding sample size calculations when designing future violence prevention cluster randomized trials in school settings - PMC
results.content: # Effect sizes and intra-cluster correlation coefficients measured from the Green Dot High School study for guiding sample size calculations when designing future violence prevention cluster randomized trials in school settings. To help guide future study planning, we provide information on anticipated effect sizes and intra-cluster correlation coefficients (ICCs), as well as school sizes, for dating violence (DV) and interpersonal violence outcomes based on data from a cRCT which evaluated the bystander-based violence intervention *‘Green Dot’*. Besides the desired significance level, power, and effect size, numerical information is needed on school sizes (number of subjects from whom data are collected) and the intra-cluster correlation coefficient (ICC) [9], which quantifies the degree of clustering. Utilizing data from the Green Dot High School (GDHS) study, we provide information on observed school sizes, effect sizes, and ICC values specific to victimization and perpetration outcomes related to sexual and dating violence in teens. In order to calculate the required number of clusters to design a cRCT to assess the efficacy of the intervention versus control, information on desired level of significance (, type II error rate (), the standard deviation of the outcome variable, the cluster size ( ; the average high school size), the ICC, and the effect size are needed. results.title: Frontiers | Adequate Sample Sizes for a Three-Level Growth Model
results.content: In multilevel modeling, sufficient sample sizes are needed to obtain unbiased estimates and enough power to detect individual or group effects. When researchers conduct a three-level growth model analysis, the question of sufficient sample size for adequate statistical power and accurate estimates of parameters arise. In this paper, simulation studies are used to examine the effects of different sample sizes at each level on the accurate estimates and adequate power in three-level growth models in which time points are nested within individuals and individuals are nested within groups. 1. What are sufficient level-1, level-2, and level-3 sample sizes for accurate parameter and standard error estimates and adequate power when estimating a three-level growth model? The question of how many individuals per group and how many groups should be sampled to obtain accurate estimates (e.g., fixed effects estimates, random effects estimates, standard errors) from two-level MLM has been addressed in several studies (Kreft, 1996; Maas and Hox, 2004, 2005; Snijders and Bosker, 2012). In conclusion, to investigate adequate sample sizes for a three-level growth model for accurate estimates and power, this study conducts a simulation under a variety of conditions. Power estimates for the fixed effect Z reached the 0.8 level with groups of a sample size of 100. The purpose of this paper was to perform simulation studies for three-level growth models and to illustrate the effect of the ICC, level-2 and level-3 sample size on the accuracy of estimates and power. First, what are sufficient level-1, level-2, and level-3 sample sizes for accurate parameter and standard error estimates and adequate power when estimating a three-level growth model? This finding aligns with the results of previous 2-level model studies that demonstrated no bias in the estimates of the fixed effects with 30 groups (Maas and Hox, 2004; Clarke, 2008; Bell et al., 2014). As previously researched, standard error estimates of group-level variance are the most influenced model estimate when the sample size is small (Maas and Hox, 2005; Clarke, 2008). This study indicates that required sample sizes can be different, according to researchers' interest in parameter estimates (i.e., fixed effect, random effect) at each level, ICC and statistical power.

results.title: Cohen's effect sizes
results.content: # Effect Size FAQs. ## Research that matters, results that make sense. ## Cohen’s effect sizes. Say you’ve got an effect size equivalent to *r* = .25. How do you interpret this effect size? Ideally you will be able to contextualize this effect against some meaningful frame of reference. But if that’s not possible another approach is to refer to conventions such as those developed by Jacob Cohen. In his authoritative *Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences*, Cohen (1988) outlined a number of criteria for gauging small, medium and large effect sizes in different metrics, as follows:. *r* effects: small ≥ .10, medium ≥ .30, large ≥ .50. *d* effects: small ≥ .20, medium ≥ .50, large ≥ .80. According to Cohen, an effect size equivalent to *r* = .25 would qualify as small in size because it’s bigger than the minimum threshold of .10, but smaller than the cut-off of .30 required for a medium sized effect. So what can we say about *r* = .25? It’s small, and that’s about it. Cohen’s conventions are easy to use. You just compare your estimate with his thresholds and get a ready-made interpretation of your result. But Cohen’s t-shirt sized conventions are somewhat arbitrary and it is not difficult to conceive of situations where a small effect observed in one setting might be considered more important than a large effect observed in another. As always, context matters when interpreting results. For more on interpreting effect sizes, see my book *Effect Size Matters*:. + Effect Size FAQs* Already have a WordPress.com account?

results.content: 9: Effect Sizes and Power Analysis. 9.2: What Are Effect Sizes? # 9.2: What Are Effect Sizes? Effect sizes are expressed as standard deviation units. ## 9.2.1: Different Effect Sizes. There are two types of effect sizes. We term this pattern as ‘mean differences among groups.’ For this pattern, the effect size we want to see is how far apart the mean scores are for each group. We term this pattern “associations.” The stronger the association between the two variables, the larger the effect size is. For mean differences between groups, we use the following effect sizes. For associations between variables, we use the following effect sizes. ## 9.2.2: Calculating Effect Sizes. The basic formula for an effect size is the following: mean (group 1) – mean (group 2) / pooled standard deviation. If there is no report of an effect size, as a rough guess of an effect size, you could subtract the difference between the two group means, take the average of the standard deviation between both groups, and do a rough division of the difference divided by the ￼. ## 9.2.3: The Range of Effect Sizes. Effect sizes are expressed as standard deviation units. I like to think of effect size as a proportion of the standard deviation. Small sample sizes produce effects, but they are hard to notice. ## 9.2.4: What Effect Sizes Do You Want to See? Ostensibly, a low effect size means that the effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable is weak. In psychology, because there are so many variables that impact an outcome, and because of imprecise measurements of our variables, research designs in psychology cannot possibly include every variable in their study; low effect sizes are bound to occur. In psychology, low effect sizes might be and should be desired. In this context, a low effect size might reflect the realities or the difficulties of how people change. ## 9.2.5: Effect Sizes and Other Considerations. *Effect sizes and the p* value*. If there is no significant pattern in the variables, it is not significant, and there are no effect sizes to detect.
